draft.title: Reading for inference
card: An inference is something a text suggests but does not state. The reader works it out from clues and adds it to what the text says.
Clues can be word choice, detail and what is left out. A character who "slams" a door shows more anger than one who "closes" it.
Example: Sam checks the clock three times, then drops his bag by the door and stares at the empty driveway. A reader can infer that he is anxious and waiting for someone.
A sound inference is backed by clues in the text. A guess with no clue behind it is not an inference. Name the clue when you explain the inference.
draft.remember: An inference is an idea you work out from clues the text gives, not one it states.

a.q: Which of these is an inference about a character, rather than a stated fact?
opts: The text says Lena walks home slowly, so she may be sad
The text says Lena walks home from school each day
The text says Lena is thirteen years old
The text says Lena carries a blue bag
a.why: Slow walking is a clue, and the reader works out a feeling the text never states. The other options only repeat facts the text gives. Facts are not inferences, even when they are about a character.
a.clue: Which option goes beyond what the text says outright?

b.q: A story says: Mia's mother asks how the match went. Mia says "Fine" and goes straight to her room. What is the best inference, and why?
opts: Mia is upset, because her short reply and exit hint at it
Mia is upset, because the text says she lost the match
Mia is tired, because her mother asks about the match
Mia is happy, because she says the word "Fine"
b.why: The short answer and leaving at once are clues that suggest Mia is upset. The text never says she lost, so that reason is made up. The word "Fine" alone does not show she is happy, because her actions point the other way.
b.clue: Look for the option that names a clue actually in the passage.

a.best: The text says Lena walks home slowly, so she may be sad

b.best: Mia is upset, because her short reply and exit hint at it

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is clearly the longest, and it is the only one with a qualifier ('so she may be sad'), while the other three are short, flat statements. A student could pick it from its form alone, without understanding inference.

check.summary: The card and question b are sound. In question a, the right option is the only long one with a hedged 'so she may be' clause, so it gives itself away. Rewording the distractors to a similar length and form would fix this.

a.q: A story says: Lena walks home slowly, kicking at stones, and does not answer when a friend calls her name. Which is an inference?
opts: Lena is troubled by something
Lena walks slowly and kicks stones
Lena failed a test at school today
Lena does not answer when called
a.why: Her slow walk, the kicked stones and her silence are clues that suggest she is troubled, though the text never says so. Walking slowly and not answering are stated outright, so they are not inferences. Nothing in the passage points to a failed test, so that is a guess.
a.clue: Find the idea the text suggests but never says, with clues behind it.
